I am not aware of concrete plans but this is interesting, let me get back to you more carefully after Strata. Of course I am aware of HAMA-601 which should open the possibility, but there's lots of streaming features we are using, so it may not be easy.


Antonio

On Wednesday, February 27, 2013 9:12:44 PM UTC-8, Edward Yoon wrote:
Hey all,

Is there any plan to use the BSP (Apache Hama) which is fit for scientific computations as a parallel computing engine, instead of MapReduce? Once Hama is integrated with Hadoop 2.0 (in near future), you'll be able to easily submit the Hama BSP job to Hadoop cluster.

Ed.

messages.author: 1969907ca50bb1fd
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#612] Re: Integrating R and Apache Hama
parts:
Hama is a BSP computing engine on top of HDFS, and YARN is a resource
manager, which manages the cluster resource allocation and multiple
(e.g., MapReduce, BSP, MPI, Spark) jobs.

See also, http://svn.apache.org/repos/asf/hama/trunk/docs/diagram/yarn-hama-diagram.pptx

In my humble opinion, BSP and MPI should be used as a main parallel
computing engine of R, instead of others (Iterative MR or Spark).

messages.author: 63023c771a070260
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#612] Re: Integrating R and Apache Hama
parts:
Is there a good example of where the BSP model is strictly more general than spark? It seems to me there should be such a thing because spark persisted data sets are read only, albeit possibly in distributed memory. For instance, with the kmeans example, that Thomas Jungblut (HAMA committer) uses on his blog, you really can't appreciate the difference between the two models, because each iteration takes in input an immutable large set of points and a smaller, mutable, broadcast set of centers. Of course there must be also some fault tolerance tradeoffs with unrestricted mutability, I am trying to wrap my mind around HAMA-503 but it will take more time.  Thanks


Antonio

messages.author: 1969907ca50bb1fd
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#617] Re: Integrating R and Apache Hama
parts:
Maybe I have to learn more about Spark's programming model and its mechanism.

BTW, it looks like Spark had been not tested on real large cluster yet
-- "The original input file is around 1G, and the job will take up as
much memory as we allocate. I have had it consume 180G per working on
4 workers."[1]

Unlike data-intensive text processing, I think almost
scientific/mathematical algorithms have one characteristic in common:
Input is relatively small but computational complexity is big. So,
we're focus more on spilling (MEM + Disk hybrid) messaging queue and
partitioning algorithms for distributing workloads of graph or matrix
computations than performance.

1. https://groups.google.com/d/topic/spark-users/3gmk3zdEZ7w/discussion
